Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person

issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, carrying a weapon is hard to reconcile clinically with the indexed trauma and the rest of the profile. It implies danger from interpersonal or environmental attack rather than illness-related threat, with no supporting triggers, memory, or appraisal content indicating assault-related fear.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: Scanning for exits and being unable to believe reassurance about safety can occur in severe PTSD, but together they suggest a persistent external attack/escape-based threat style that fits poorly with a life-threatening illness trauma unless there is clear accompanying illness-specific danger content. No such illness-linked threat items are present.

issues.item: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
issues.explanation: The profile is clinically incoherent because it omits Triggers and Memory entirely despite an extreme PTSD severity (PCL-5=73) and instead concentrates on severe Threat, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies without any plausible illness-linked intrusion or cue structure.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is poorly matched to a life-threatening illness trauma and points toward an assault/accident-type fear context rather than medical trauma; this clashes with 'Avoid Medical Cues' which is the trauma-congruent avoidance item.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: 'Dissociate Deliberately' is possible in PTSD, but paired here with strongly illness-specific avoidance and no memory/trigger content, it suggests a different symptom profile and lacks support from the stated formulation, which centers Threat–Appraisal–Strategy cycling rather than dissociative disengagement.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is not well aligned with the trauma type of life-threatening illness. The example implies a threat context more typical of assault/accident trauma, while the rest of the profile centers on medical cues.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Medical Cues' and 'Avoid Thinking' fit illness trauma, but 'Avoid Circumstances ... being in the dark' pulls toward a different trauma context, reducing within-node coherence.

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: Cross-node coherence is weakened because the threat items emphasize generalized danger and delays, while the negative appraisals are purely global self-defectiveness/weakness with no illness-related or health-related meaning. For life-threatening illness, some link is expected between medical threat and appraisals; these items instead suggest a different or more diffuse formulation.

vignette:
Kiet Phanthavong is a 35-year-old Laotian-American UX designer who lives with his wife in a mid-sized city in the Pacific Northwest. He was referred for psychological assessment following a reluctant disclosure to his primary care physician - made only because his wife had quietly asked the doctor to ask - that he had not been sleeping well and had been "off" since his hospitalisation two years prior. By the time Kiet sat across from a therapist for the first time, his PCL-5 score of 73 placed him in the severe range, though he was visibly uncomfortable with the idea that a physical illness could leave the kind of mark that warranted a mental health referral. He had come, he said, mostly to reassure his wife.

Two years earlier, Kiet had been admitted to the ICU after a previously undetected cardiac arrhythmia triggered a sudden collapse at his desk during a remote work call. He had been alone in the apartment at the time. He regained partial consciousness on the floor to find his vision narrowing, his chest seizing in a way he could not distinguish from dying, and no certainty whatsoever about whether help was coming. The paramedics arrived within minutes, but those minutes - the cold floor, the sound of his own laboured breathing, the absolute absence of control - had not resolved themselves into a past event. They had settled into him.

In the weeks following his discharge, Kiet found that the sight of an ambulance on his commute could drop him back onto that floor without warning. He began taking longer routes to avoid the hospital district, rationalising this as a preference for less congested streets. When his cardiologist scheduled a six-week follow-up, Kiet cancelled and did not reschedule. He told himself he felt fine. What he could not tell himself - because it was too large and too shapeless - was that walking back through those automatic doors felt like confirmation of something he was not ready to confirm. He has not had a physical examination since discharge.

At work, where Kiet spends long hours building user interfaces that are meant to feel intuitive and frictionless, the environment has become its own kind of minefield. When a design file takes longer than usual to load, or when a client delays feedback beyond the agreed window, something in him shifts immediately into a register that has nothing to do with the task at hand. He had come to believe, in a way that felt utterly rational to him, that delays meant something had gone wrong - that the pause before a response was the pause before bad news. He would refresh the screen, check his email, message the client, and be unable to explain to his colleagues why he seemed so agitated over a slow server. Even when his project lead assured him that the timeline was fine, Kiet found it impossible to absorb that reassurance. Safety, as others described it, felt like a story told about someone else's life.

His body remained in a state of low-grade readiness that exhausted him. He had stopped going to the gym, where the elevation of his heart rate now frightened him in a way he could not fully articulate but would not risk. He and his wife had stopped hiking, something they had done most weekends before his illness. She had not complained. He was grateful for that, and also aware that her patience was its own kind of weight.

What concerned Kiet most, and what he found hardest to say aloud, was that he no longer felt like himself in any way he could point to. He described feeling hollow in the sessions - present in rooms but not quite in them, going through the motions of a life that used to feel like his. He had come to believe there was something fundamentally broken in him, not medically but essentially, and that his inability to simply move on from an illness that had been treated and resolved was evidence of a weakness he found humiliating. He had survived. He believed he should be fine. The gap between those two facts was where he lived now, and what finally brought him to treatment was the quiet fear, shared with no one until now, that the gap was getting wider.
